summary:
The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation, and the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court. Sexual-orientation discrimination was banned in 1996, making South Africa the first country to do so; marriage equality followed with the Civil Union Act of 2006; legal gender recognition has been available since the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003; and the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024 explicitly protects sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics.

On 14 November 2025 the Gauteng High Court, sitting as an Equality Court, delivered judgment in Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (case 2024/070075), a challenge brought against the Department of Correctional Services with the assistance of Lawyers for Human Rights. The court held that refusing a transgender inmate prescribed gender-affirming health care falls below the required standard of health care, and that refusing feminising clothing and accessories is likewise unlawful. Orders compelling the Department to provide hormone treatment at state expense, permit clothing and cosmetics expressing the inmate's gender identity, implement the accommodations required by its own standard operating procedure for transgender inmates, and deliver prescribed medical care were granted. The South African Human Rights Commission's National Preventive Mechanism welcomed the ruling the same day.

Correctional Services already had a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners before the ruling; reporting in August 2025 recorded that rights organisations doubt whether it is implemented in practice. Detention therefore remains a site of elevated risk for trans visitors and residents despite the binding remedies now in place.

Outside prison, everyday exposure is shaped by documents. The Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act requires medical evidence, a pathologising route that locks people out of legal gender recognition, and its binary sex classification excludes non-binary people altogether; reform toward self-determination is pending but not in force. Costs of affirming one's gender through the process are described as dauntingly high. Where documents do not match presentation, trans people face humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for alleged fraud. A 2024 Gender Dynamix report documents a trans woman who was met with police mockery and refused when she attempted to file a domestic-violence complaint after producing her identity document.

Violence risk is documented and ongoing. On 26 December 2024 Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old trans woman and make-up artist, survived an unprovoked hate-crime assault at a tavern in Tshwane that left her with severe facial injuries and lasting physical and emotional scars; she spoke out publicly and an arrest was reported. OUT LGBT Well-being's rights watch for December 2024 recorded five LGBTQIA+ murders that month. Violence disproportionately affects Black lesbian, trans and gender-nonconforming people in townships.

Access to gender-affirming care is uneven. Activists in East London delivered a memorandum to Frere Hospital over treatment delays running to a year. Academic analysis published in 2024 examining whether the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act read with section 9 of the Constitution prohibits the exclusion of transgender and non-binary people from gender-segregated bathrooms concludes that trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in facility access, so restroom and changing-room disputes remain foreseeable for visitors.
tangentialFactors:
The trajectory of state recognition runs back more than a decade: Justice Minister Jeff Radebe launched a programme against gender-based and LGBTI violence citing the Constitution's equality clause, an early government framing of LGBTI violence as a policy problem that preceded the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024.

South Africa's statutory package compares with the small group of jurisdictions combining constitutional sexual-orientation protections, statutory gender recognition, marriage equality and an operative equality court; the divergence between that package and enforcement is the pattern the Mokoena litigation and the Frere Hospital memorandum illustrate.

The prison ruling is a data point within a wider correctional pattern rather than an isolated finding: a standard operating procedure existed, implementation was contested by practitioners, and a court then ordered the Department of Correctional Services to comply with its own rules.

Academic and civil-society debate continues over whether legal gender recognition should be reframed as a right grounded in dignity rather than a medical procedure, and over the exclusion of non-binary identities from a binary marker system.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition under the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act requires medical documentation, and applicants bear the financial cost of the medical and legal steps involved; the process is described in domestic commentary as prohibitively expensive for many applicants.

Only two sex markers are available on official documents, so non-binary residents have no route to a matching marker through the existing statute, and reform toward self-determination has been proposed but is not yet law.

Residents who present with documents that do not align with their appearance report being refused service and threatened with arrest for fraud, and Gender Dynamix's 2024 report records police mocking a trans woman who sought to open a domestic-violence case.

Residents in correctional facilities are covered by the Department of Correctional Services standard operating procedure for transgender inmates and, since the Equality Court judgment of 14 November 2025, by court orders requiring hormone treatment at state expense, gender-expressive clothing and the delivery of prescribed care.

Township residents, particularly Black lesbian, trans and gender-nonconforming people, bear a disproportionate share of the recorded violence, and community organisations reported five LGBTQIA+ murders in December 2024 alone.

Public healthcare for trans residents is available but unevenly delivered, with documented treatment delays of up to a year prompting direct action against a provincial hospital in the Eastern Cape.
outOfScopeNotes:
The extent to which the Department of Correctional Services standard operating procedure is implemented across facilities after the November 2025 orders is not resolved by the available sources; rights organisations expressed doubt before the ruling and no post-ruling compliance reporting is available here.

Whether exclusion from gender-segregated bathrooms constitutes unfair discrimination remains an open question: the source is a 2024 academic analysis of the issue rather than a reported court holding, and no binding precedent on facility access is sourced.

The status and timing of the pending reform toward self-determining legal gender recognition, and whether the medical requirements will be removed, are not sourced and should be checked against current legislation before travel.

Whether the 2024 Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act has produced prosecutions in cases involving gender identity is not evidenced in the inventory, so its enforcement record remains unverified here.

Sentencing outcomes in the Tshwane tavern assault and the identity of those detained in the December 2024 killings are not sourced beyond the report of an arrest.
